DahKrmJ2JD0.speaker_note: Session 14 of his own Sunday Al-Ahzab series; one voice, continues directly from the previous session.
DahKrmJ2JD0.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 14: Remember Allah Much (33:41-44)
DahKrmJ2JD0.one_line: Why the command to remember Allah abundantly sits amid the surah's hardest stories, and how dhikr removes distress at Allah's commands.
DahKrmJ2JD0.summary: He recaps the surah's theme: obedience when it is uncomfortable, through the Trench, the Prophet's wives and Zaynab's marriage. Between these private stories come verses on the Prophet's status, and here the command to remember Allah much. He explains why it is placed here: dhikr is the remedy for distress at a command. He teaches the sequence of reasoning, ruling and benefit, with pork, travelling with a mahram and intoxication as examples, and argues that dhikr is the reasoning behind salah and other worship. Dhikr works on two levels. Thinking of Allah before every decision makes His commands familiar, so a ruling on interest or relationships does not shock you after years of the opposite. Regular tasbih morning and evening attaches the heart, as the hizb and wird did for earlier Muslims. He gives a practical routine of 300 phrases morning and evening, urges keeping a private act known only to Allah, and explains tasbih, istighfar, hamd and la ilaha illallah, with the hadith of the card that outweighs ninety-nine scrolls. Dhikr must show in behaviour. Allah and His angels send blessings on those who remember Him, bringing them from darkness to light, and their greeting on meeting Him is peace, the opposite of distress.

outline.heading: A surah of stories found nowhere else
outline.gist: The Trench, the Prophet's wives and the Zayd and Zaynab story occur only in Al-Ahzab, which makes its theme unique.

outline.heading: The theme: obeying when it is hard (33:36)
outline.gist: The surah views submission from many angles, above all obeying when it is awkward; some commands are appreciated at once, others only years later or on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Recap: the Trench and the wives
outline.gist: The Muslims' greatest fear at the Trench, then the wives unhappy with the Prophet's chosen poverty and the issues of women in the deen.

outline.heading: Recap: the Zaynab marriage and no distress
outline.gist: The most uncomfortable episode of his life; the lesson that a believer should feel no distress at what Allah commands.

outline.heading: His private life on display, and verses on his status
outline.gist: Four stories expose the Prophet's home; between them Allah places verses on his status so no one thinks he is being belittled.

outline.heading: Whenever he is corrected, his status follows
outline.gist: His lapses were choices of a lesser priority, not sins like ours, and the Quran follows them with his praise, as after the month he withdrew from his wives.

outline.heading: How we avoid distress at Allah's commands
outline.gist: These are the easiest verses of the series, and perhaps the most important, because they answer how to avoid the distress the Prophet felt.

outline.heading: Recitation of 33:41-44
outline.gist: He recites the passage.

outline.heading: The dhikr command placed amid the hardest stories
outline.gist: One of the most important commands in the Quran sits in a surah of heavy, controversial stories.

outline.heading: Three kinds of hard command
outline.gist: Courage when you want to run, accepting poverty, and socially awkward acts such as praying where others can see you.

outline.heading: Remember Him much: counted tasbih
outline.gist: Every command of dhikr in the Quran comes with abundance; the traditional way is counting tasbih, some reaching tens of thousands a day.

outline.heading: Reminding yourself of Allah through the day
outline.gist: The second way: consulting Allah first in decisions, reactions, speech and what you look at, instead of living on habit.

outline.heading: Dhikr is the purpose of salah (20:14)
outline.gist: Allah told Musa to establish prayer for His remembrance; when Allah states a reason for a command, that reason is untouchable.

outline.heading: Reasoning, ruling, benefit: the pork example
outline.gist: Rulings flow one way from their reasoning; benefits are not the reason, and pork, given no stated reason, stays forbidden whatever the pig's diet.

outline.heading: The mahram rule and its reasoning of safety
outline.gist: A woman travelled with a mahram for safety; where travel is safe the reasoning is gone, but in a war zone the ruling returns.

outline.heading: Intoxication: recreational versus medical
outline.gist: The reasoning is recreational intoxication, so all drugs are forbidden while anaesthesia in surgery is not.

outline.heading: Dhikr as the reasoning behind worship
outline.gist: Dhikr is the reason behind many acts of worship, salah first, and the few minutes a day standing before Allah are the best a person can hope for.

outline.heading: "Keep your tongue moist with remembrance"
outline.gist: A man found Islam's laws too many and asked for one thing to hold on to; the answer was dhikr, and its absence leaves you spiritually dry.

outline.heading: Soil that dries too long
outline.gist: Like sand, a heart left dry for too long may stop responding to water at all.

outline.heading: Level one: Allah in every decision
outline.gist: If you always ask what Allah wants before acting, His commands are familiar and a ruling never feels alien.

outline.heading: Why rulings on interest or relationships shock people
outline.gist: Those deep in interest-bearing contracts or forbidden relationships feel distress at the answer and look for another sheikh, because they did not remember Allah beforehand.

outline.heading: Back to 33:36: no choice, but no distress
outline.gist: You need not enjoy a command, but there should be no distress in following it.

outline.heading: Level two: tasbih morning and evening
outline.gist: Repeated glorification attaches the heart to Allah's name.

outline.heading: The hizb and the wird
outline.gist: Every Muslim historically had a daily portion of Quran and a portion of dhikr, and made them up if missed.

outline.heading: A routine to try
outline.gist: Fatihah, Ayat al-Kursi, the morning verses, then 100 istighfar, 100 salawat and 100 la ilaha illallah morning and night for a few months.

outline.heading: Closeness makes commands make sense
outline.gist: Interest being forbidden makes no sense to someone far from Allah; draw closer and commands you struggle with change in how they look.

outline.heading: Try it and see the difference
outline.gist: Even 600 a day will improve prayer, stability and acceptance of commands; this is the Quran's most explicit dhikr command.

outline.heading: Dhikr with presence that shows in life
outline.gist: Mindless repetition while doing harm is a split faith; know what you say and carry it into your choices.

outline.heading: Keep a secret between you and Allah
outline.gist: Have one private act no one knows of, to guard sincerity; dhikr is the easiest to hide.

outline.heading: Ubayy and how much salawat to make
outline.gist: Asked how much of his prayer to give to salawat, the Prophet kept saying more is better until Ubayy said all of it, and was told his worries would be removed and sins forgiven.

outline.heading: Those who struggle without dhikr
outline.gist: Many struggle with prayer, Quran, anger, depression and lack of purpose; dhikr is the reasoning behind all private worship.

outline.heading: Istighfar as dhikr
outline.gist: Seeking forgiveness acknowledges a sin, resolves not to return and plans to become better.

outline.heading: Tasbih: declaring Allah free of imperfection
outline.gist: Other faiths give God a son, human emotions or limits; tasbih declares that nothing resembles Him in any attribute.

outline.heading: Why the ego resists tasbih
outline.gist: The nafs wants to be the greatest and so tries to bring God down; when life knocks you flat, a well-rooted subhanallah keeps you from blaming Him.

outline.heading: The believers at the Trench
outline.gist: Seeing the Confederates, the hypocrites called it a lie while the believers said this is what Allah promised, and it only increased their faith.

outline.heading: Why we do dhikr together
outline.gist: In congregation, one sincere voice may carry the rest whose sincerity falls short.

outline.heading: Alhamdulillah: practical optimism
outline.gist: There is always something to thank Allah for, even being alive; not seeing it is dangerous.

outline.heading: Make dhikr central: before you speak
outline.gist: Find 10 to 15 minutes a day; remembering Allah before cursing someone or snapping at your wife makes you a person people love to be around.

outline.heading: La ilaha illallah: the ID card
outline.gist: The word you hope will save you on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: The card that outweighs ninety-nine scrolls
outline.gist: A man with ninety-nine scrolls of sins is shown one card bearing la ilaha illallah, said once with sincerity, and it outweighs them all.

outline.heading: No guarantee, so say it often
outline.gist: This is not promised to you; renew your faith by saying la ilaha illallah, and say dhikr without needing to be prompted.

outline.heading: Dhikr must turn into action
outline.gist: If tongue and heart produce no visible change, something is broken; the hadith is not a soothing excuse to stop working.

outline.heading: He and His angels send blessings on you
outline.gist: When you remember Him, Allah sends His mercy and blessing and the angels pray for you, as in 40:7.

outline.heading: From darkness into light
outline.gist: Allah brings those who remember Him out of darkness into light, in this world and the next; He is especially merciful to believers.

outline.heading: Their greeting is peace
outline.gist: Peace is the opposite of the distress the surah speaks of; found through dhikr in this life, it continues on meeting Allah and in Paradise.

themes.label: Dhikr: remembrance of Allah
themes.note: Dhikr in two forms, Allah in every decision and regular tasbih, as the remedy for distress at commands and the reasoning behind worship.

themes.label: Obedience to Allah and the Messenger

themes.label: Obedience to Allah and the Messenger

themes.label: The purposes behind Allah's commands (maqasid)

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example

33:26.ar: وَأَنزَلَ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَٰهَرُوهُم مِّنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ مِن صَيَاصِيهِمۡ وَقَذَفَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلرُّعۡبَ فَرِيقࣰ ا تَقۡتُلُونَ وَتَأۡسِرُونَ فَرِيقࣰ ا
33:26.en: And He brought those of the People of the Scripture who supported them down from their strongholds, and cast panic into their hearts. Some ye slew, and ye made captive some

33:27.ar: وَأَوۡرَثَكُمۡ أَرۡضَهُمۡ وَدِيَٰرَهُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلَهُمۡ وَأَرۡضࣰ ا لَّمۡ تَطَـُٔوهَاۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرࣰ ا
33:27.en: And He caused you to inherit their land and their houses and their wealth, and land ye have not trodden. Allah is ever Able to do all things

33:28.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِيُّ قُل لِّأَزۡوَٰجِكَ إِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدۡنَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَزِينَتَهَا فَتَعَالَيۡنَ أُمَتِّعۡكُنَّ وَأُسَرِّحۡكُنَّ سَرَاحࣰ ا جَمِيلࣰ ا
33:28.en: O Prophet! Say unto thy wives: If ye desire the world's life and its adornment, come! I will content you and will release you with a fair release

33:29.ar: وَإِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدۡنَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ وَٱلدَّارَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ أَعَدَّ لِلۡمُحۡسِنَٰتِ مِنكُنَّ أَجۡرًا عَظِيمࣰ ا
33:29.en: But if ye desire Allah and His messenger and the abode of the Hereafter, then lo! Allah hath prepared for the good among you an immense reward

33:30.ar: يَٰنِسَآءَ ٱلنَّبِيِّ مَن يَأۡتِ مِنكُنَّ بِفَٰحِشَةࣲ مُّبَيِّنَةࣲ يُضَٰعَفۡ لَهَا ٱلۡعَذَابُ ضِعۡفَيۡنِۚ وَكَانَ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيرࣰ ا
33:30.en: O ye wives of the Prophet! Whosoever of you committeth manifest lewdness, the punishment for her will be doubled, and that is easy for Allah

33:31.ar: ۞وَمَن يَقۡنُتۡ مِنكُنَّ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَتَعۡمَلۡ صَٰلِحࣰ ا نُّؤۡتِهَآ أَجۡرَهَا مَرَّتَيۡنِ وَأَعۡتَدۡنَا لَهَا رِزۡقࣰ ا كَرِيمࣰ ا
33:31.en: And whosoever of you is submissive unto Allah and His messenger and doeth right, We shall give her her reward twice over, and We have prepared for her a rich provision

33:21.ar: لَّقَدۡ كَانَ لَكُمۡ فِي رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ أُسۡوَةٌ حَسَنَةࣱ لِّمَن كَانَ يَرۡجُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَٱلۡيَوۡمَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَ وَذَكَرَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرࣰ ا
33:21.en: Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much

XdoZP051oQA.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 10 (33:26-31)
XdoZP051oQA.one_line: Accepting the uncomfortable Qurayzah ruling, the Prophet's wives choosing a life of simplicity, divorce done beautifully, and why higher status doubles the stakes.
XdoZP051oQA.summary: He first returns to Banu Qurayzah, a ruling many Muslims find hard to discuss: the tribe betrayed Medina in wartime, surrendered out of panic, and asked for Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's judgment. He notes reported execution numbers range from 40 to 900, from a study he did as a student, and leans toward the lower figure, but insists the point is to submit even when a ruling does not suit your personal narrative; you must follow everything without having to enjoy everything. He then opens the next section. As wealth grew, the Prophet's wives asked for more provision; he withdrew for a month, Umar wept at the mat marks on his body and empty shelves, and verses 28-29 gave the wives a choice between the worldly life with a generous, gracious divorce, or Allah, His Messenger and the Hereafter. He distinguishes the dunya, which is neutral, from a life of low desires, and condemns the cultural use of divorce as a weapon, calling for civil separations and continued support. All the wives chose the Prophet. He challenges couples to ask whether their marriages rest only on a promise of financial improvement. Verses 30-31 double both punishment and reward for the wives, illustrating that greater status brings greater responsibility, which applies to born Muslims and to the scholar, donor and martyr who acted for show.

outline.heading: Every uncomfortable episode is in this surah
outline.gist: He returns to the last verses because Al-Ahzab addresses each difficult situation in the seerah.

outline.heading: Why the Qurayzah ruling troubles people
outline.gist: The executions and expulsion seem to clash with the Prophet's character; the surah raises it precisely to require submission.

outline.heading: Follow it all without having to enjoy it all
outline.gist: Agree with the fundamentals; you need not love every detail, just as a child need not enjoy every instruction.

outline.heading: Betrayal in wartime and the siege
outline.gist: Qurayzah nearly caused the annihilation of the Muslims; besieged twenty nights, they had supplies for a year while the Muslims had little.

outline.heading: Panic, surrender and the request for Sa'd's judgment
outline.gist: Fear made the people surrender against their leaders' advice, and they asked to be judged by their old ally Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.

outline.heading: Sa'd's ruling and the disputed numbers
outline.gist: Combatants who committed treason were executed and the rest evacuated; reports range from 40 to 900, and he leans to the lower figures.

outline.heading: Submitting when the reason is discomfort, not fear
outline.gist: The surah will show obedience made hard by reasons other than fear.

outline.heading: A new chapter: wealth increases
outline.gist: Around the fifth to seventh year Muslims grew wealthier, and the Prophet's wives expected their situation to improve.

outline.heading: The wives and their tiny homes
outline.gist: Low mud rooms with nothing stored; he names the nine wives, of different tribes and backgrounds.

outline.heading: Exceptional women who united the tribes
outline.gist: His marriages bound tribes to the message; each wife's story should be taught to our daughters.

outline.heading: He came home empty-handed
outline.gist: However large his share of spoils, the Prophet gave it away before reaching home.

outline.heading: The wives ask for more
outline.gist: They agreed together to ask; Abu Bakr and Umar told their daughters to ask them instead.

outline.heading: A month's withdrawal and a rumour of divorce
outline.gist: Deeply upset, he vowed to stay away for a month; Medina feared he had divorced them all.

outline.heading: Umar asks permission three times
outline.gist: Turned away twice, Umar was admitted and found the Prophet lying on a coarse mat.

outline.heading: Umar weeps at the empty shelves
outline.gist: The mat had marked his body and almost no food was stored, while foreign kings lived in luxury.

outline.heading: "Theirs is this world, ours the Hereafter"
outline.gist: The Prophet rebuked Umar for measuring things by money.

outline.heading: Umar lightens the mood: he had not divorced them
outline.gist: Umar joked about the women of Medina speaking back, and confirmed there was no divorce.

outline.heading: The verses brought to each wife
outline.gist: After twenty-nine days he recited them to each wife and told them to consult their parents before answering.

outline.heading: Recitation of verses 28-29
outline.gist: The two verses of choice.

outline.heading: Dunya versus the worldly life
outline.gist: The dunya is a neutral time frame needed for the Hereafter; al-hayat ad-dunya is a way of life built on low desires.

outline.heading: Showing off and the adornments of this life
outline.gist: Displaying what we have, often indirectly, hurts others.

outline.heading: "Come, I will provide for you"
outline.gist: Mut'ah here means giving them the provision they want, and also the support owed after divorce.

outline.heading: A beautiful release
outline.gist: Sarah jamil means parting civilly, with no insults or exposing secrets.

outline.heading: Throwing out the cultural view of divorce
outline.gist: Divorce is not a weapon to keep a wife in line; it is a decision to end a marriage that cannot work, without smearing or refusing to co-parent.

outline.heading: Divorce with beautiful patience
outline.gist: Like sabr jamil, he hopes Muslim men will part calmly and support their ex-wives financially.

outline.heading: How the Prophet would have divorced
outline.gist: He never divorced, but this verse shows how he would have: providing for her and keeping secrets.

outline.heading: Choosing Allah, His Messenger and the Hereafter
outline.gist: A great reward awaits those who do good; Aisha answered immediately without needing to consult her parents.

outline.heading: Every wife chose him
outline.gist: He was not poor but selflessly generous, and treated his wives exactly as he treated himself.

outline.heading: Would we make that choice?
outline.gist: Accepting a low financial and social status for life is a hard form of submission, for women and men alike.

outline.heading: Marriages built on a promise of financial improvement
outline.gist: Couples always wait for the raise, the house, the second car; would the marriage still be happy if that hope ended?

outline.heading: He chose to have nothing
outline.gist: His family never ate three days in a row by his choice, which is not required of us.

outline.heading: So no one has an excuse not to follow him
outline.gist: Unlike kings such as Sulayman and Dawud, his poverty removes any excuse that he was well off.

outline.heading: The wives became distributors of charity
outline.gist: Afterwards he brought money home and the wives distributed it to people.

outline.heading: A difficulty as hard as fear
outline.gist: Giving up hope of a better life by choice may be even harder than facing an army.

outline.heading: Recitation of verses 30-31: the contract
outline.gist: The first of two addresses to the wives continues the agreement they made.

outline.heading: A public major sin punished double
outline.gist: Fahishah mubayyinah is a clear, public major sin; for the wives it would bring a double punishment.

outline.heading: Higher status, higher responsibility
outline.gist: When your possible reward is higher, your possible punishment is greater too; the door opens equally both ways.

outline.heading: Double reward and a unique provision
outline.gist: Obedience and good deeds bring twice the reward; karim here means unique.

outline.heading: Why the stakes were doubled for the wives
outline.gist: They bore a hard life with the Prophet and represented him and Islam.

outline.heading: The same law for those born Muslim
outline.gist: Raised with Islam, we have a higher ceiling for reward and a deeper floor for punishment than those who were not.

outline.heading: The scholar, the donor and the martyr thrown in first
outline.gist: Those who did great deeds for status are the first into the Fire because their potential reward was so high.

outline.heading: Outro

33:28.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِيُّ قُل لِّأَزۡوَٰجِكَ إِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدۡنَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَزِينَتَهَا فَتَعَالَيۡنَ أُمَتِّعۡكُنَّ وَأُسَرِّحۡكُنَّ سَرَاحࣰ ا جَمِيلࣰ ا
33:28.en: O Prophet! Say unto thy wives: If ye desire the world's life and its adornment, come! I will content you and will release you with a fair release

33:29.ar: وَإِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدۡنَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ وَٱلدَّارَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ أَعَدَّ لِلۡمُحۡسِنَٰتِ مِنكُنَّ أَجۡرًا عَظِيمࣰ ا
33:29.en: But if ye desire Allah and His messenger and the abode of the Hereafter, then lo! Allah hath prepared for the good among you an immense reward

33:30.ar: يَٰنِسَآءَ ٱلنَّبِيِّ مَن يَأۡتِ مِنكُنَّ بِفَٰحِشَةࣲ مُّبَيِّنَةࣲ يُضَٰعَفۡ لَهَا ٱلۡعَذَابُ ضِعۡفَيۡنِۚ وَكَانَ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيرࣰ ا
33:30.en: O ye wives of the Prophet! Whosoever of you committeth manifest lewdness, the punishment for her will be doubled, and that is easy for Allah

33:31.ar: ۞وَمَن يَقۡنُتۡ مِنكُنَّ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَتَعۡمَلۡ صَٰلِحࣰ ا نُّؤۡتِهَآ أَجۡرَهَا مَرَّتَيۡنِ وَأَعۡتَدۡنَا لَهَا رِزۡقࣰ ا كَرِيمࣰ ا
33:31.en: And whosoever of you is submissive unto Allah and His messenger and doeth right, We shall give her her reward twice over, and We have prepared for her a rich provision

33:32.ar: يَٰنِسَآءَ ٱلنَّبِيِّ لَسۡتُنَّ كَأَحَدࣲ مِّنَ ٱلنِّسَآءِ إِنِ ٱتَّقَيۡتُنَّۚ فَلَا تَخۡضَعۡنَ بِٱلۡقَوۡلِ فَيَطۡمَعَ ٱلَّذِي فِي قَلۡبِهِۦ مَرَضࣱ وَقُلۡنَ قَوۡلࣰ ا مَّعۡرُوفࣰ ا
33:32.en: O ye wives of the Prophet! Ye are not like any other women. If ye keep your duty (to Allah), then be not soft of speech, lest he in whose heart is a disease aspire (to you), but utter customary speech

33:33.ar: وَقَرۡنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ وَلَا تَبَرَّجۡنَ تَبَرُّجَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِيَّةِ ٱلۡأُولَىٰۖ وَأَقِمۡنَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتِينَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَطِعۡنَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥٓۚ إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ لِيُذۡهِبَ عَنكُمُ ٱلرِّجۡسَ أَهۡلَ ٱلۡبَيۡتِ وَيُطَهِّرَكُمۡ تَطۡهِيرࣰ ا
33:33.en: And stay in your houses. Bedizen not yourselves with the bedizenment of the Time of Ignorance. Be regular in prayer, and pay the poor-due, and obey Allah and His messenger. Allah's wish is but to remove uncleanness far from you, O Folk of the Household, and cleanse you with a thorough cleansing

33:34.ar: وَٱذۡكُرۡنَ مَا يُتۡلَىٰ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ لَطِيفًا خَبِيرًا
33:34.en: And bear in mind that which is recited in your houses of the revelations of Allah and wisdom. Lo! Allah is Subtile, Aware

2:235.ar: وَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ فِيمَا عَرَّضۡتُم بِهِۦ مِنۡ خِطۡبَةِ ٱلنِّسَآءِ أَوۡ أَكۡنَنتُمۡ فِيٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡۚ عَلِمَ ٱللَّهُ أَنَّكُمۡ سَتَذۡكُرُونَهُنَّ وَلَٰكِن لَّا تُوَاعِدُوهُنَّ سِرًّا إِلَّآ أَن تَقُولُواْ قَوۡلࣰ ا مَّعۡرُوفࣰ اۚ وَلَا تَعۡزِمُواْ عُقۡدَةَ ٱلنِّكَاحِ حَتَّىٰ يَبۡلُغَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبُ أَجَلَهُۥۚ وَٱعۡلَمُوٓاْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا فِيٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡ فَٱحۡذَرُوهُۚ وَٱعۡلَمُوٓاْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌ حَلِيمࣱ‏
2:235.en: There is no sin for you in that which ye proclaim or hide in your minds concerning your troth with women. Allah knoweth that ye will remember them. But plight not your troth with women except by uttering a recognised form of words. And do not consummate the marriage until (the term) prescribed is run. Know that Allah knoweth what is in your minds, so beware of Him; and know that Allah is Forgiving, Clement

3:154.ar: ثُمَّ أَنزَلَ عَلَيۡكُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ ٱلۡغَمِّ أَمَنَةࣰ نُّعَاسࣰ ا يَغۡشَىٰ طَآئِفَةࣰ مِّنكُمۡۖ وَطَآئِفَةࣱ قَدۡ أَهَمَّتۡهُمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ يَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ غَيۡرَ ٱلۡحَقِّ ظَنَّ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِيَّةِۖ يَقُولُونَ هَل لَّنَا مِنَ ٱلۡأَمۡرِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۗ قُلۡ إِنَّ ٱلۡأَمۡرَ كُلَّهُۥ لِلَّهِۗ يُخۡفُونَ فِيٓ أَنفُسِهِم مَّا لَا يُبۡدُونَ لَكَۖ يَقُولُونَ لَوۡ كَانَ لَنَا مِنَ ٱلۡأَمۡرِ شَيۡءࣱ مَّا قُتِلۡنَا هَٰهُنَاۗ قُل لَّوۡ كُنتُمۡ فِي بُيُوتِكُمۡ لَبَرَزَ ٱلَّذِينَ كُتِبَ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡقَتۡلُ إِلَىٰ مَضَاجِعِهِمۡۖ وَلِيَبۡتَلِيَ ٱللَّهُ مَا فِي صُدُورِكُمۡ وَلِيُمَحِّصَ مَا فِي قُلُوبِكُمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
3:154.en: Then, after grief, He sent down security for you. As slumber did it overcome a party of you, while (the other) party, who were anxious on their own account, thought wrongly of Allah, the thought of ignorance. They said: Have we any part in the cause? Say (O Muhammad): The cause belongeth wholly to Allah. They hide within themselves (a thought) which they reveal not unto thee, saying: Had we had any part in the cause we should not have been slain here. Say: Even though ye had been in your houses, those appointed to be slain would have gone forth to the places where they were to lie. (All this hath been) in order that Allah might try what is in your breasts and prove what is in your hearts. Allah is Aware of what is hidden in the breasts (of men)

5:50.ar: أَفَحُكۡمَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِيَّةِ يَبۡغُونَۚ وَمَنۡ أَحۡسَنُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ حُكۡمࣰ ا لِّقَوۡمࣲ يُوقِنُونَ
5:50.en: Is it a judgment of the time of (pagan) ignorance that they are seeking? Who is better than Allah for judgment to a people who have certainty (in their belief)

48:26.ar: إِذۡ جَعَلَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ ٱلۡحَمِيَّةَ حَمِيَّةَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِيَّةِ فَأَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ سَكِينَتَهُۥ عَلَىٰ رَسُولِهِۦ وَعَلَى ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَأَلۡزَمَهُمۡ كَلِمَةَ ٱلتَّقۡوَىٰ وَكَانُوٓاْ أَحَقَّ بِهَا وَأَهۡلَهَاۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيۡءٍ عَلِيمࣰ ا
48:26.en: When those who disbelieve had set up in their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Age of Ignorance, then Allah sent down His peace of reassurance upon His messenger and upon the believers and imposed on them the word of self-restraint, for they were worthy of it and meet for it. And Allah is Aware of all things

gkh6_vFN2Ko.speaker: adnan
gkh6_vFN2Ko.speaker_note: eleventh session of his Sunday Al-Ahzab tafseer series; continues his own sequence
gkh6_vFN2Ko.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 11 (33:32-34)
gkh6_vFN2Ko.one_line: Privilege as responsibility, not flirting, finding joy at home, tabarruj and the four jahiliyyahs, and the wives as Ahl al-Bayt.
gkh6_vFN2Ko.summary: After recapping the wives' choice and the double reward and punishment, he explains verse 32. 'You are not like other women' should be read as extra responsibility, not privilege; treating any blessing as an honour before it is rewarded on the Day of Judgment is a subtle arrogance. Taqwa is a preventive system, and part of it is not softening one's speech, which he explains at length as flirting: indirect, coded friendliness through tone, laughter and compliments that builds attraction while staying deniable. Married people do it too, being charming outside and harsh at home. Since even the mothers of the believers were taught this, no one should assume children will simply know; he urges parents to teach daughters and sons to stay professional, save warmth for spouses, and to see that real joy comes from freedom from desires. In verse 33 he favours reading qarna as finding the coolness of your eye at home, making the home the place everyone loves to be. He defines tabarruj as deliberately displaying what need not be shown, relative to a community's dress code, and maps the Quran's four uses of jahiliyyah onto theological, political, social and chastity ethics. He argues the verse names the wives as Ahl al-Bayt, notes their role in transmitting the Prophet's teaching, and ends with Allah as Al-Latif, Al-Khabir.

outline.heading: Recap: the cluster and Al-Ahzab's angle
outline.gist: Obedience in the most difficult, awkward and frightening situations.

outline.heading: Recap: the battle section
outline.gist: The surah commented on everyone's reactions, from the best to the worst.

outline.heading: Recap: the wives' choice and a wife's right to ask
outline.gist: A wife has the right to ask for a better life, and if he cannot provide it he should let her go graciously.

outline.heading: Husbands' obligations and a marriage without financial hope
outline.gist: Men must meet their wives' financial, social and emotional needs; staying with no prospect of improvement was a hard obedience.

outline.heading: Recap: double reward and double punishment
outline.gist: The privileged are punished more for sins and rewarded more for good.

outline.heading: Recitation of verse 32
outline.gist: The second address to the wives of the Prophet.

outline.heading: "You are not like other women": where to pause
outline.gist: Some read it as a standalone statement, others join it to 'if you have taqwa'.

outline.heading: Privilege or responsibility?
outline.gist: We prefer readings that flatter us; until the Day of Judgment every blessing should be treated as extra responsibility.

outline.heading: Claiming blessings as honour is subtle arrogance
outline.gist: Assuming Allah gave you more because you are better may cause deeds to be rejected; possessions are weight on your back.

outline.heading: What was specific to the Prophet and his household
outline.gist: Some rulings, like marrying more than four, applied only to him; he will point out which verses are specific.

outline.heading: The wives would represent him and Islam
outline.gist: Revealed about five years before his death, the verses prepared them to become the mothers of the believers.

outline.heading: The mothers of the believers as teachers
outline.gist: Aisha and Umm Salamah used their status to teach and narrate, roles women had not held before.

outline.heading: Taqwa as a preventive system
outline.gist: Taqwa is a long-term system for keeping harm out of the self and society.

outline.heading: What 'softening speech' means: flirting
outline.gist: Not obscene or direct, but a coded under-layer of tone, body language, laughter and compliments.

outline.heading: Flirting is deniable by design
outline.gist: Colleagues talk about work, neighbours about shared living; flirting can always be denied.

outline.heading: Married people flirt too
outline.gist: Spouses notice it even when nothing wrong is said.

outline.heading: How attraction builds toward the haram
outline.gist: No one proposes sin directly; attraction grows slowly until modesty is the only barrier left; the wives were taught etiquette, not accused.

outline.heading: "Lest the one with a diseased heart become hopeful"
outline.gist: The second mention of diseased hearts in the surah; purifying the heart runs through its theme.

outline.heading: How men read the signals
outline.gist: A smile or tone becomes hope; mixed signals confuse and cause problems.

outline.heading: Teach your daughters to stay professional
outline.gist: Be a colleague, student or teacher, keep to the point and give no false under-layer; this never excuses harassment.

outline.heading: Speak words that are right
outline.gist: Qawl ma'ruf is polite, proper speech; discussing marriage is fine if it stays proper, otherwise go through intermediaries.

outline.heading: General command or specific to the wives?
outline.gist: Because it is conditioned on taqwa, which everyone can practise, the command applies to all women and men.

outline.heading: Double stakes, same command
outline.gist: Only the doubled punishment is specific to the wives, not the command itself.

outline.heading: Do not assume anyone knows: teach it
outline.gist: If even the mothers of the believers had to be told, our youth must be taught explicitly.

outline.heading: A system to prevent zina in communities
outline.gist: Flirting becomes normal unless someone points it out; prevention needs explicit adab.

outline.heading: Save the warmth for your spouse
outline.gist: Be professional, not mean, with others; extra friendliness belongs to engagement and marriage.

outline.heading: Charming outside, harsh at home
outline.gist: Many men are sweet to other women and cold to their wives because this was never taught.

outline.heading: Why it starts with women, and the man's guilt
outline.gist: Biology makes women's conduct decisive for whether zina spreads, but a man who becomes hopeful has a diseased heart and cannot blame her.

outline.heading: "You've killed all the fun": real joy is liberty
outline.gist: That road ends in pain and broken families; real enjoyment needs sobriety and freedom from enslaving desires.

outline.heading: Recitation of verse 33
outline.gist: Qarna is one of the most debated words in the Quran.

outline.heading: Qarna as 'stay in your homes'
outline.gist: One wife understood it this way and stayed home after the Prophet's death; Aisha did not, and led a very active life.

outline.heading: Qarna as 'find the coolness of your eye at home'
outline.gist: He prefers this reading, from qurrat al-'ayn: make the home the place you most enjoy.

outline.heading: Tabarruj: deliberately displaying what need not be shown
outline.gist: Tabarruj is judged against a community's dress code, so it differs in the West; explain this to daughters when they compare themselves to friends.

outline.heading: The four jahiliyyahs of the Quran
outline.gist: The word appears only four times, always attached to a behavior.

outline.heading: Theological, political, social and ethical ignorance
outline.gist: False assumptions about Allah, rule by ignorance, tribal zealotry or racism, and tabarruj as an ethical failing.

outline.heading: Chastity ethics as their own category
outline.gist: Islam treats chastity ethics separately from general ethics like honesty and loyalty because different forces drive them.

outline.heading: Dress in pre-Islamic Arabia
outline.gist: The spectrum was wide: enslaved women barely covered, people circling the Ka'bah almost naked, noble women veiled.

outline.heading: Khadijah: a merchant of spotless chastity
outline.gist: Known as the pure one, she dealt with men constantly in business without anyone questioning her conduct.

outline.heading: The 'former jahiliyyah'
outline.gist: Scholars place it as early as Adam's sons or between Nuh and Idris, or just before the Prophet.

outline.heading: A home people love keeps families strong

0Xf4dQnxbq8.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 4 (33:7-9)
0Xf4dQnxbq8.one_line: The heavy covenant of the prophets, being questioned about our claimed truthfulness, and the opening of the Battle of the Trench narrative.
0Xf4dQnxbq8.summary: He recaps that Al-Ahzab opens a cluster of surahs on submission to Allah, approached through situations where obeying is hard. Verses 7-8 transition from the opening examples into the battle story: Allah took a heavy covenant from all prophets, naming the five strong-willed messengers because the surah is about commands that demand strength of will. A heavy covenant carries real difficulty, yet commands bring ease both now and later, like studying for exams; people struggle with delayed reward. Verse 8 says even the truthful will be questioned about their truthfulness, so faith is a claim that life must prove, and it is proven most in hardship. He criticizes those who vanish from the masjid when life gets hard, and warns that feeling safe from Allah's punishment is a major sin since no one knows which deeds were accepted. He then sets the historical scene of the Confederates: the coalition of ten thousand, Salman's trench idea, Medina's geography, and the digging. Verse 9 opens with the ending, the wind and unseen forces, and stresses that Allah watches behavior, not results. He closes by explaining why these verses, which contain criticism of some companions, are rarely taught, and insists we learn from them without lowering the companions' status.

outline.heading: Why the opening verses took several sessions
outline.gist: He explains he spent several lessons on the first six verses to establish the surah's theme and context.

outline.heading: Al-Ahzab: obedience when the command is hard
outline.gist: The surah opens a cluster on submission, looking at obedience when the situation or the command is difficult, with the Prophet as the prime example.

outline.heading: Recap of zihar, adoption and inheritance
outline.gist: He reviews the three opening examples of uncomfortable rulings and notes that the Ahzab story fills nearly 30% of the surah.

outline.heading: The covenant taken from the prophets: mithaq versus 'ahd
outline.gist: A mithaq is a pledge reinforced with oaths, heavier than an ordinary covenant.

outline.heading: Parallel covenant in Aal Imran: all prophets would follow Muhammad
outline.gist: He links the verse to 3:81 and the hadith that Musa would have to follow the Prophet, showing the universality of his message.

outline.heading: The five strong-willed messengers named together
outline.gist: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad appear together only here and in Ash-Shura; they are named because the surah is about commands that need strong will.

outline.heading: A heavy covenant that carries difficulty
outline.gist: Ghaliz means thick and heavy: obedience will not always be easy or serve short-term interests.

outline.heading: Commands bring ease now and later
outline.gist: Like studying for exams, obeying is hard in the moment but yields ease in this life and the next.

outline.heading: Delayed gratification and the children's candy study
outline.gist: People want reward now; the ability to wait for delayed reward is central to understanding the deen and teaching it to youth.

outline.heading: The truthful will be questioned about their truthfulness
outline.gist: Faith is a claim; Allah will examine it, so feeling sincere inside is not enough.

outline.heading: "This is between Me and My servant"
outline.gist: The hadith qudsi on Al-Fatihah: your claim to worship Him alone will be shown by how you live.

outline.heading: Faith shines brightest in hardship
outline.gist: Like true friends, true faith shows when life turns hard; he criticizes people who leave the masjid when they struggle.

outline.heading: Reading the book of your own life
outline.gist: On the Day of Judgment you read your record and judge whether it sounds like someone who worshipped Allah alone.

outline.heading: Patience is at the first strike
outline.gist: The hadith of the grieving woman: your first reaction to hardship shows whether you are on the right path.

outline.heading: Complacency: feeling safe from Allah's punishment
outline.gist: Centuries of 'say the shahadah and relax' bred laziness; no one knows whether any deed was accepted.

outline.heading: Two fears or two securities are never combined
outline.gist: Whoever fears Allah in this life is safe on the Day of Gathering, and whoever feels safe now will fear then; he also explains the word ahzab.

outline.heading: Background: Badr, Uhud and the exiled tribe
outline.gist: After the setback at Uhud, a leader of the expelled Jewish tribe toured Arabia rallying tribes against Medina.

outline.heading: An unprecedented coalition of ten thousand
outline.gist: Tribes of different backgrounds united for the first time; the Prophet learned early through his informants and expected overwhelming numbers.

outline.heading: Consultation and Salman's trench idea
outline.gist: The Prophet consulted the companions and adopted a Persian tactic, showing their flexibility in accepting an idea from a rival culture.

outline.heading: Medina's geography and digging the trench
outline.gist: Lava fields east and west, Banu Qurayzah's forts to the south, so a five-kilometre trench was dug in the north in about ten days.

outline.heading: A frightened city, and a story told from its ending
outline.gist: Only about 1,500 fighters, scarce food; the Quran begins with the outcome then goes back through the incidents.

outline.heading: Junud: those who carry out Allah's purposes
outline.gist: The word means more than armed soldiers; it is any creation sent to serve His command, and only He knows them.

outline.heading: The trench standoff
outline.gist: The Confederates found the trench impassable; the fighting was mostly arrows across it.

outline.heading: Daily fear and the danger from the south
outline.gist: One breach or a betrayal by Banu Qurayzah would end everything; the siege lasted over twenty days.

outline.heading: The wind, and his own desert sandstorm
outline.gist: Allah ended it simply with wind; he recalls a sandstorm on the Medina-Makkah road in 1997.

outline.heading: The wind wrecks the Confederate camp
outline.gist: The Muslims were sheltered by their earth barricade while the open camp lost tents, fire and belongings; Hudhayfah saw huge pots carried by the wind.

outline.heading: Allah watches the behavior, we watch the result
outline.gist: The ending is given first so the focus moves to what the believers did during the siege.

outline.heading: Why the name Al-Basir here
outline.gist: Allah chose the name tied to seeing because He wants to see the action that testifies to the claimed faith.

outline.heading: Proving love in a moment of fear
outline.gist: A husband who abandons his wife in danger can never repair it; people who stand together in hardship form unbreakable bonds.

outline.heading: What the Quran tells and what it leaves out
outline.gist: The verses skip the trench details and focus on what people did; he urges reading ahead before next week.

outline.heading: Learning from the companions' mistakes: Hudhayfah's reply
outline.gist: These verses criticize some companions, so they are rarely taught; Hudhayfah told a later man he could not judge what he had not lived.

outline.heading: Outro

7eHj8Qh59sU.title: Tafseer of Surat al-Kahf, Session 18: Dhul-Qarnayn Builds the Barrier
7eHj8Qh59sU.one_line: Dhul-Qarnayn builds the barrier against Gog and Magog: power used to give, teach and empower rather than take.
7eHj8Qh59sU.summary: He finishes the story of Dhul-Qarnayn as the surah's picture of a people who have gathered idea, wealth and knowledge and therefore hold real power. The story shows what such power is for: Dhul-Qarnayn travels to distant strangers, sees what each lacks and gives it, never conquering, enslaving or exploiting. He counts five peoples in the story and asks which one Muslims are today, answering that we resemble the people between the two mountains: numbers, wealth and a book, but no practical knowledge or organisation to protect ourselves. Dhul-Qarnayn refuses payment, asks them to work alongside him, gives a stronger solution than they asked for, and openly teaches them the process of iron, fire and molten copper so they can maintain it themselves. From this he draws lessons on excellence, investing time, not monopolising knowledge, and not fighting other people's fights for them, whether nations or a bullied child. When the barrier holds he credits his Lord's mercy, unlike Qarun, and reminds them nothing stands forever. He closes by recapping the surah's journey and arguing that a strong, giving community is the best da'wah; the threats invading our homes today come through screens and mentalities, and our main product must be the human being.

outline.heading: Recap: all elements together produce true power
outline.gist: The previous stories covered idea, wealth and knowledge; Dhul-Qarnayn had them all, plus numbers, and so held real power.

outline.heading: Power means giving, not taking
outline.gist: To distant strangers he offered whatever they lacked, law, wealth or knowledge, rather than seizing what they had.

outline.heading: Two horns: holding both sides of every duality
outline.gist: Power and justice, material and spiritual, law and numbers; he grasped the bull by both horns.

outline.heading: Power is dangerous: how history's strong treated the weak
outline.gist: Most powerful civilisations brought oppression and bloodshed; Dhul-Qarnayn is the counter-example.

outline.heading: Five peoples in the story
outline.gist: His own people with everything, the lawless rich, the destitute, the people lacking know-how, and the corrupt Gog and Magog.

outline.heading: Which people are we?
outline.gist: Muslims most resemble the third group: we have the idea, wealth and numbers but lack practical knowledge and will to act.

outline.heading: The first two peoples revisited
outline.gist: He gave law to the first group and material help to the second.

outline.heading: Between two mountains: speaking over their heads
outline.gist: He spoke of faith, society and civilisation at a high level and they barely understood, like youth hearing such talk today.

outline.heading: A people with everything except the know-how to defend itself
outline.gist: They had numbers, money and law but could not protect themselves from Gog and Magog, symbols of chaos, and offered tribute for a barrier.

outline.heading: Interlude
What my Lord has established me with: power as a natural result
outline.gist: Power is not obtained artificially but follows naturally from ideology, wealth and practical knowledge, giving a community a voice and representation.

outline.heading: Refusing their money
outline.gist: He declined payment; he asks when a nation ever protected another for free.

outline.heading: Help me with your strength: doing it with them
outline.gist: He would not do it for them or hand over a manual; he required them to participate and shared all he knew.

outline.heading: A radm: a double barrier, better than they asked
outline.gist: They asked for a single wall; he built two barriers with fill between, far harder to breach.

outline.heading: Iron sheets between the cliffs and the bellows
outline.gist: He had them bring iron, level the gap between the cliffs and blow the fire, a step-by-step process he taught them.

outline.heading: Molten copper and doing the job perfectly
outline.gist: The Quran describes physics, chemistry, teamwork and management; worship includes doing work properly, supervised and double-layered.

outline.heading: He invested his time and kept no secret ingredient
outline.gist: He stayed until it was done and taught them so they could repair it later against periodic raids.

outline.heading: They asked for one thing; he gave many
outline.gist: A better solution, participation and teaching, so they could hold off a far larger enemy after he left.

outline.heading: Punishing the lawless versus protecting the weak
outline.gist: Answering a question, he contrasts the first people's internal oppression, which needed law, with this people's external threat.

outline.heading: Do not fight other people's fights
outline.gist: He would not wage their war; toppling dictators with foreign troops only replaces one with another, so give people the tools instead.

outline.heading: Parenting: the bullied child
outline.gist: If you punch every bully for your child, the child never learns to look after himself.

outline.heading: Metallurgy then; what is missing today
outline.gist: Liquefying metals was advanced knowledge he did not withhold; today the book, numbers, money and expertise exist, so why does our good not reach others?

outline.heading: You cannot give what you do not have
outline.gist: A struggling community cannot offer anything; building strength is the best da'wah.

outline.heading: Were Gog and Magog proven guilty?
outline.gist: In discussion he notes the whole community testified, and he only taught them protection rather than punishing anyone.

outline.heading: Leaving the signs of the Hour for another time
outline.gist: The many opinions on Gog and Magog at the end of time are a separate study; some views of the signs breed passivity.

outline.heading: Neither over it nor through it
outline.gist: The two verb forms differ: climbing over is easier than boring through, and he had sealed both routes.

outline.heading: This is a mercy from my Lord, unlike Qarun
outline.gist: He stayed to watch the raid fail and credited Allah, where Qarun claimed his success came from his own knowledge.

outline.heading: Nothing stands forever; Gog and Magog surge
outline.gist: He humbled the celebrating people with the reminder that every structure falls, while the raiders turned on each other.

outline.heading: The surah's journey from cave to civilisation
outline.gist: From youths defining their values, through wealth in the two gardens and knowledge with al-Khidr, to a strong society that gives.

outline.heading: Why he roamed the earth
outline.gist: He went to the far west, far east and remote mountains searching for people who needed the good Allah gave him.

outline.heading: This is what Islam is supposed to look like
outline.gist: Reading this weekly should embarrass us; Muslim history had ups and downs in different regions, and it can rise again.

outline.heading: Money is the easiest fix; law and knowledge are hardest
outline.gist: Lack of wealth is the simplest problem; we struggle to run institutions or give our children a proud Islamic identity.

outline.heading: Today's external threats come through screens
outline.gist: Our raiders invade homes through media and mentalities; Muslims should offer a globalisation of giving, not domination.

outline.heading: Give, and Allah increases your means
outline.gist: Knowing what it is to need, the blessed give, and Allah multiplies their means.

outline.heading: Build communities in the West; the product is the person
outline.gist: With the Muslim world at a low point, Western communities can become working examples, investing in the human being.

outline.heading: Read it every week; the best da'wah
outline.gist: Look each week for something to work on; a giving, strong community is better da'wah than any talk.

outline.heading: Outro

33:18.ar: ۞قَدۡ يَعۡلَمُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنكُمۡ وَٱلۡقَآئِلِينَ لِإِخۡوَٰنِهِمۡ هَلُمَّ إِلَيۡنَاۖ وَلَا يَأۡتُونَ ٱلۡبَأۡسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
33:18.en: Allah already knoweth those of you who hinder, and those who say unto their brethren: "Come ye hither unto us!" and they come not to the stress of battle save a little

33:19.ar: أَشِحَّةً عَلَيۡكُمۡۖ فَإِذَا جَآءَ ٱلۡخَوۡفُ رَأَيۡتَهُمۡ يَنظُرُونَ إِلَيۡكَ تَدُورُ أَعۡيُنُهُمۡ كَٱلَّذِي يُغۡشَىٰ عَلَيۡهِ مِنَ ٱلۡمَوۡتِۖ فَإِذَا ذَهَبَ ٱلۡخَوۡفُ سَلَقُوكُم بِأَلۡسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ أَشِحَّةً عَلَى ٱلۡخَيۡرِۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ لَمۡ يُؤۡمِنُواْ فَأَحۡبَطَ ٱللَّهُ أَعۡمَٰلَهُمۡۚ وَكَانَ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيرࣰ ا
33:19.en: Being sparing of their help to you (believers). But when the fear cometh, then thou (Muhammad) seest them regarding thee with rolling eyes like one who fainteth unto death. Then, when the fear departeth, they scald you with sharp tongues in their greed for wealth (from the spoil). Such have not believed. Therefor Allah maketh their deeds fruitless. And that is easy for Allah

33:20.ar: يَحۡسَبُونَ ٱلۡأَحۡزَابَ لَمۡ يَذۡهَبُواْۖ وَإِن يَأۡتِ ٱلۡأَحۡزَابُ يَوَدُّواْ لَوۡ أَنَّهُم بَادُونَ فِي ٱلۡأَعۡرَابِ يَسۡـَٔلُونَ عَنۡ أَنۢبَآئِكُمۡۖ وَلَوۡ كَانُواْ فِيكُم مَّا قَٰتَلُوٓاْ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا
33:20.en: They hold that the clans have not retired (for good); and if the clans should advance (again), they would fain be in the desert with the wandering Arabs, asking for the news of you; and if they were among you, they would not give battle, save a little

33:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَةَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِذۡ جَآءَتۡكُمۡ جُنُودࣱ فَأَرۡسَلۡنَا عَلَيۡهِمۡ رِيحࣰ ا وَجُنُودࣰ ا لَّمۡ تَرَوۡهَاۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ بَصِيرًا
33:9.en: O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see. And Allah is ever Seer of what ye do

33:10.ar: إِذۡ جَآءُوكُم مِّن فَوۡقِكُمۡ وَمِنۡ أَسۡفَلَ مِنكُمۡ وَإِذۡ زَاغَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡصَٰرُ وَبَلَغَتِ ٱلۡقُلُوبُ ٱلۡحَنَاجِرَ وَتَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ ٱلظُّنُونَا۠
33:10.en: When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when eyes grew wild and hearts reached to the throats, and ye were imagining vain thoughts concerning Allah

33:11.ar: هُنَالِكَ ٱبۡتُلِيَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ وَزُلۡزِلُواْ زِلۡزَالࣰ ا شَدِيدࣰ ا
33:11.en: There were the believers sorely tried, and shaken with a mighty shock

33:12.ar: وَإِذۡ يَقُولُ ٱلۡمُنَٰفِقُونَ وَٱلَّذِينَ فِي قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضࣱ مَّا وَعَدَنَا ٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُۥٓ إِلَّا غُرُورࣰ ا
33:12.en: And when the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, were saying: Allah and His messenger promised us naught but delusion

33:13.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَت طَّآئِفَةࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ يَٰٓأَهۡلَ يَثۡرِبَ لَا مُقَامَ لَكُمۡ فَٱرۡجِعُواْۚ وَيَسۡتَـٔۡذِنُ فَرِيقࣱ مِّنۡهُمُ ٱلنَّبِيَّ يَقُولُونَ إِنَّ بُيُوتَنَا عَوۡرَةࣱ وَمَا هِيَ بِعَوۡرَةٍۖ إِن يُرِيدُونَ إِلَّا فِرَارࣰ ا
33:13.en: And when a party of them said: O folk of Yathrib! There is no stand (possible) for you, therefor turn back. And certain of them (even) sought permission of the Prophet, saying: Our homes lie open (to the enemy). And they lay not open. They but wished to flee

33:14.ar: وَلَوۡ دُخِلَتۡ عَلَيۡهِم مِّنۡ أَقۡطَارِهَا ثُمَّ سُئِلُواْ ٱلۡفِتۡنَةَ لَأٓتَوۡهَا وَمَا تَلَبَّثُواْ بِهَآ إِلَّا يَسِيرࣰ ا
33:14.en: If the enemy had entered from all sides and they had been exhorted to treachery, they would have committed it, and would have hesitated thereupon but little

33:16.ar: قُل لَّن يَنفَعَكُمُ ٱلۡفِرَارُ إِن فَرَرۡتُم مِّنَ ٱلۡمَوۡتِ أَوِ ٱلۡقَتۡلِ وَإِذࣰ ا لَّا تُمَتَّعُونَ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا
33:16.en: Say: Flight will not avail you if ye flee from death or killing, and then ye dwell in comfort but a little while

33:17.ar: قُلۡ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِي يَعۡصِمُكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ إِنۡ أَرَادَ بِكُمۡ سُوٓءًا أَوۡ أَرَادَ بِكُمۡ رَحۡمَةࣰۚ وَلَا يَجِدُونَ لَهُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَلِيࣰّ ا وَلَا نَصِيرࣰ ا
33:17.en: Say: Who is he who can preserve you from Allah if He intendeth harm for you, or intendeth mercy for you. They will not find that they have any friend or helper other than Allah

49:14.ar: ۞قَالَتِ ٱلۡأَعۡرَابُ ءَامَنَّاۖ قُل لَّمۡ تُؤۡمِنُواْ وَلَٰكِن قُولُوٓاْ أَسۡلَمۡنَا وَلَمَّا يَدۡخُلِ ٱلۡإِيمَٰنُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمۡۖ وَإِن تُطِيعُواْ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ لَا يَلِتۡكُم مِّنۡ أَعۡمَٰلِكُمۡ شَيۡـًٔاۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمٌ
49:14.en: The wandering Arabs say: We believe. Say (unto them, O Muhammad): Ye believe not, but rather say "We submit," for the faith hath not yet entered into your hearts. Yet, if ye obey Allah and His messenger, He will not withhold from you aught of (the reward of) your deeds. Lo! Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

18:105.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ رَبِّهِمۡ وَلِقَآئِهِۦ فَحَبِطَتۡ أَعۡمَٰلُهُمۡ فَلَا نُقِيمُ لَهُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ وَزۡنࣰ ا
18:105.en: Those are they who disbelieve in the revelations of their Lord and in the meeting with Him. Therefor their works are vain, and on the Day of Resurrection We assign no weight to them

moRT2tu-T58.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 7 (33:18-20)
moRT2tu-T58.one_line: Those who discourage others from good, cowardice and stinginess, Ali's duel with Amr ibn Wudd, and why Allah never generalizes.
moRT2tu-T58.summary: He opens by explaining that the Quran revisits a few principles from many angles, and that obedience does not require liking every command. After recapping the hypocrites' conduct at the trench, he focuses on a word found only here: those who discourage others from doing good. People discourage others either because they could not do it themselves or because they think it wrong, and he warns families and communities against fear-based discouragement about marriage, careers, activism or friendships. Real advice lays out the information, as a doctor presents data, and real support means backing someone whose choice you would not make. Allah describes these people as cowardly and stingy, yet says 'except a little', never denying all good in them, which he turns into a strong warning against generalizing about any group. Verse 19 describes fear coming and going for everyone; he contrasts the hypocrites' rolling eyes with Ali's courage and modesty in his duel with Amr ibn Wudd. When fear left, the hypocrites spoke with sharp tongues and grabbed for spoils, so their deeds were voided, which should make every believer humble and anxious that their deeds be accepted. Verse 20 shows them unable to believe the Confederates had gone, wishing they were among the Bedouins.

outline.heading: A few principles seen from many angles
outline.gist: Religion is a small set of fundamentals; the Quran is a clear book, not a complicated one.

outline.heading: Why the Quran repeats an idea through examples
outline.gist: Each angle gives a precedent you can draw a parallel to when you face a similar situation.

outline.heading: You need not like a command to follow it
outline.gist: Obedience does not require agreeing with or enjoying every ruling; its wisdom may become clear later.

outline.heading: Recap: the Confederates and the believers' first reaction
outline.gist: Ten thousand from many tribes; the Quran leaves the believers' assumptions unstated out of respect.

outline.heading: Recap: the hypocrites' words and desertion
outline.gist: Calling the promise a delusion, urging people home and claiming exposed houses.

outline.heading: Recap: what they would have done, and the two groups
outline.gist: Open hypocrites and Muslims with diseased hearts would both have sold out had the city fallen.

outline.heading: Recap: the two convictions
outline.gist: Fleeing does not extend life and no one protects you from Allah.

outline.heading: Bad thoughts are normal; deal with them
outline.gist: Even prophets had thoughts they corrected; we are accountable for speech, influence and action.

outline.heading: Words that appear only once reveal a surah's theme
outline.gist: From his own research, unique words are clues to what a surah is about; he recites verse 18.

outline.heading: "Allah indeed knows"
outline.gist: With Allah as subject, qad before a present-tense verb is emphasis, not rarity.

outline.heading: Al-mu'awwiqin: those who discourage others
outline.gist: A word found nowhere else in the Quran: not merely failing to do good but holding others back from it.

outline.heading: Why people discourage others
outline.gist: Either they wish they could do it and want company in not doing it, or they are convinced it is wrong; both harm society.

outline.heading: "Come to us": leave Muhammad to be devoured
outline.gist: The deserters invited their brothers home, predicting Abu Sufyan's army would wipe the defenders out.

outline.heading: "Except a little": Allah never generalizes
outline.gist: Generalizing about a whole group is the height of ignorance; Allah does not deny all good even in them.

outline.heading: The voice of goodness that remains; lacking courage
outline.gist: A voice of reason always remains inside; standing for what is right sometimes demands courage.

outline.heading: Ashihhah: stingy with their help
outline.gist: From shuhh: withholding good from others; they would not even defend the city they had pledged to protect.

outline.heading: Discouragement in families and communities
outline.gist: We discourage marriages, careers and community involvement out of fear, with no clear basis.

outline.heading: Advice means presenting information, not opinion
outline.gist: Like a doctor laying out outcomes, advice shows the angles; the clearly halal and haram aside, most choices are grey areas.

outline.heading: True support is backing a choice you would not make
outline.gist: Supporting people only when they do what you want is easy; supporting a different choice makes you grow.

outline.heading: Fear-based parenting and 'playing it safe'
outline.gist: As a father and educator he warns against limiting children to doctor, engineer or lawyer out of inherited financial fear.

outline.heading: Carrying the sin of those you discouraged
outline.gist: Discouraging others from the right thing adds their failure to your account.

outline.heading: Recitation of verse 19: when fear comes
outline.gist: Fear rises and falls through the chaos of war.

outline.heading: Fear strikes everyone
outline.gist: The verse is general: believers and hypocrites alike felt fear; no companion was fearless that day.

outline.heading: Amr ibn Wudd's challenge
outline.gist: As defenders thinned, Arabia's most feared warrior crossed into the trench and mocked the Muslims for refusing to duel.

outline.heading: Ali volunteers and the Prophet's dua
outline.gist: Ali asked three times; the Prophet gave him his sword and shield and prayed Allah not leave him alone after losing family at Badr and Uhud.

outline.heading: Ali's three offers
outline.gist: Ali offered Amr Islam, leaving, or combat.

outline.heading: The duel and the turn in morale
outline.gist: After a fierce fight hidden by dust, Ali emerged victorious; Muslim morale soared and helped hold the trench.

outline.heading: Why Ali did not take the legendary armour
outline.gist: Victors stripped the dead until Islam forbade it; Ali left Amr's prized shield behind.

outline.heading: Ali's modesty
outline.gist: Amr's body was exposed when he fell, and Ali turned away rather than look at what was forbidden.

outline.heading: Eyes rolling as if fainting from death
outline.gist: The hypocrites stared at the Prophet in terror, as if to blame him.

outline.heading: Cowards blame the leader for a plan they accepted
outline.gist: Those who agreed to a plan turn on the leader when it goes wrong, running from responsibility.

outline.heading: Some were companions who later repented
outline.gist: The point is not to condemn them but to learn, including from their repentance.

outline.heading: When fear leaves: tongues of steel
outline.gist: Salaqukum is a verb the Quran coined: they lashed out with sharp, eloquent words about their bravery.

outline.heading: Opportunists greedy for the spoils
outline.gist: Stingy with good yet demanding equal share of the bounty, they move with whatever profits them.

outline.heading: They did not truly believe
outline.gist: Like the Bedouins told to say 'we submitted', claiming faith is only the first step.

outline.heading: Deeds made worthless
outline.gist: Habata means deeds rendered void; their conduct that day failed to prove their claim.

outline.heading: Why believers fear their deeds being rejected
outline.gist: No one knows which deeds are accepted, which is why people say 'may Allah accept' after prayer.

outline.heading: Humility before Allah
outline.gist: Allah often rewards what we did not deserve; the prophets begged for acceptance.

outline.heading: Recitation of verse 20: they think the Confederates have not gone
outline.gist: Their fear was so deep they could not believe the army had left.

outline.heading: "Now we go to them"
outline.gist: The Prophet declared the Confederates would never attack again; from then on the Muslims would go to them.

outline.heading: Childlike fear adults must outgrow
outline.gist: A child fears the dark after the light is on; adults must learn to control such instincts and teach children to do so.

33:5.ar: ٱدۡعُوهُمۡ لِأٓبَآئِهِمۡ هُوَ أَقۡسَطُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِۚ فَإِن لَّمۡ تَعۡلَمُوٓاْ ءَابَآءَهُمۡ فَإِخۡوَٰنُكُمۡ فِي ٱلدِّينِ وَمَوَٰلِيكُمۡۚ وَلَيۡسَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ جُنَاحࣱ فِيمَآ أَخۡطَأۡتُم بِهِۦ وَلَٰكِن مَّا تَعَمَّدَتۡ قُلُوبُكُمۡۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣰ ا رَّحِيمًا

PswVYdsB0nA.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ahzab, Session 12 (33:35-36)
PswVYdsB0nA.one_line: Verse 35's ten pairs establish equal responsibility and reward for men and women; verse 36 says believers do not pick and choose Allah's commands.
PswVYdsB0nA.summary: After a recap, he presents verse 35 as its own chapter, revealed when Asma bint Umays, Umm Salamah, Umm Umarah and other women asked why the Quran seemed to address only men. The Quran itself answered by listing ten pairs, masculine and feminine, covering every category of the religion: entering Islam, belief, obedience, honesty, patience, inner devotion, charity, fasting, chastity and remembrance, with identical forgiveness and reward. Different rulings reflect different roles on one team, rooted in biology, not unequal worth. He rejects both those who erase every difference and those who bring patriarchal culture into Islam, and attacks double standards on chastity and women's money that drive daughters away. Remembrance means consulting Allah before decisions, not after. Jihad is missing from the list because it is a way of life, and women took part in every battle, like Nusaybah at Uhud. Verse 36, which he calls the surah's central verse, says believers have no choice once Allah and His Messenger decide. People may dislike a ruling and voice their struggle, but must follow it, whereas communities often tolerate disobedience as long as no one complains. Finding worship hard can be a sign of faith. He asks parents to examine their own cherry-picking, then begins the story of Zayd ibn Harithah and his marriage to Zaynab.

outline.heading: Reading the long verse in one breath
outline.gist: His childhood teacher set breath challenges; this verse was the third level and took him a year.

outline.heading: Recap: the surah's theme and the battle section

outline.heading: Recap: the wives' choice
outline.gist: The Prophet chose a simple life so we could follow him; his wives were offered a gracious divorce or a life without financial hope.

outline.heading: Asma bint Umays asks: does the Quran speak of women?
outline.gist: Returning from Abyssinia, she asked whether any revelation addressed women; the question is not new.

outline.heading: Umm Salamah, Umm Umarah and a group of women ask the same
outline.gist: Four separate narrations give the same reason for the verse's revelation.

outline.heading: The answer: there is no difference
outline.gist: More famous men in history explains more mentions of men; what is said to one gender applies to the other.

outline.heading: Why he left out men's tabarruj last time
outline.gist: The verse confirms that addresses to women also include men, and vice versa.

outline.heading: Ten pairs and how Arabic plurals work
outline.gist: Arabic uses the masculine plural for mixed groups; the verse spells out both forms to remove all doubt.

outline.heading: The Quran answered, not the Prophet
outline.gist: In none of the four narrations did the Prophet reply himself; the verse came as the answer.

outline.heading: A chapter of a single verse
outline.gist: He sees verse 35 as its own chapter on the question of women in Islam and other Abrahamic faiths.

outline.heading: Recitation and the etiquette of resuming
outline.gist: When pausing in a list, one should repeat the previous pair on resuming.

outline.heading: Every category of the religion is listed
outline.gist: There is no part of the deen in which men and women do not share equal responsibility.

outline.heading: Different rulings, different roles: the team analogy
outline.gist: Defenders and attackers carry equal responsibility for the team's success but are judged by different criteria.

outline.heading: Biology assigns roles; that is not sexism
outline.gist: A man will never be a mother; religion reflecting that is natural, even if some dislike their role.

outline.heading: Religion misused to oppress women
outline.gist: It happens and is not Islamic; Muslims should address it from within rather than waiting for outsiders.

outline.heading: The Quran does rank some groups
outline.gist: It says those who strive are not equal to those who sit back, and tending the Ka'bah is not equal to faith and striving; here it says the opposite.

outline.heading: Islam, iman and devout obedience
outline.gist: Entering the faith, the same beliefs, and qunut as willing obedience.

outline.heading: Truthfulness and patience
outline.gist: The same basic ethics and values for both.

outline.heading: Humble devotion, while Europe debated women's souls
outline.gist: Khushu' refers to the inner relationship with Allah; at the time Europe still debated whether women had souls.

outline.heading: Charity: a woman's money is her own
outline.gist: Both give charity; the cultural idea that a wife must ask permission to use her own money is wrong.

outline.heading: Fasting: physically demanding worship for both
outline.gist: Men cannot claim that physical strength makes women exempt.

outline.heading: Chastity is not only a woman's duty
outline.gist: The Middle Eastern saying that a boy carries no shame contradicts the verse; roles differ but the responsibility is shared.

outline.heading: Double standards drive daughters away
outline.gist: Young women rebel when held to rules their brothers ignore; that is cultural, not Islamic.

outline.heading: Remembering Allah before every decision
outline.gist: Dhikr here means checking decisions against Allah's plan beforehand, not asking whether it was halal afterwards.

outline.heading: The same forgiveness and great reward
outline.gist: Both sin and both are forgiven; the reward is identical.

outline.heading: The reference point for every masculine plural
outline.gist: Whenever the Quran uses the masculine plural, refer back to this verse.

outline.heading: Why jihad is not in the list
outline.gist: Jihad means striving, wrongly reduced to fighting; it is a way of life, not a category of worship.

outline.heading: Jihad as the summit of the religion
outline.gist: Striving against the self, Shaytan and corruption is how the best Muslim lives.

outline.heading: Women in every battle; Nusaybah at Uhud
outline.gist: The Prophet planned to station women on rooftops; Umm Umarah defended him and was gravely wounded.

outline.heading: Both extremes are wrong
outline.gist: Denying any difference and importing patriarchal culture both distort the religion.

outline.heading: Question: equal in this life or the next?
outline.gist: Responsibilities in this life are paired and outcomes in the Hereafter are equal; roles differ by ability.

outline.heading: Question: roles by aptitude
outline.gist: Why force someone into a role they are less suited for, like a short player in basketball?

outline.heading: Question: is any worldly reward promised?
outline.gist: Only a good, meaningful life; results in this world depend on where you sit on history's curve.

outline.heading: Why ten pairs rather than one
outline.gist: Listing ten distinct pairs draws attention to the roles we play in this life, not only to equal reward.

outline.heading: The most uncomfortable episode for the Prophet
outline.gist: Had he hidden any revelation, he would have hidden verse 37; he recites verse 36.

outline.heading: No believing man or woman has a choice
outline.gist: Once Allah and His Messenger decide a matter, believers of both genders may not choose otherwise.

outline.heading: Khiyarah: the word for choice
outline.gist: A rare Arabic form from khayr, meaning choice.

outline.heading: "Is hijab an option?"
outline.gist: Being Muslim is an option; once chosen, every choice must align with it or the choice is invalid.

outline.heading: Free to choose, but believers do not pick and choose
outline.gist: No one is forced, but 'when I'm ready' and 'it's optional' are ways of refusing; men and women are equal here too.

outline.heading: The central verse of the surah
outline.gist: Whether things are hard, uncomfortable or disliked, the obligation stands.

outline.heading: You may dislike it, but you must follow it
outline.gist: Voicing a struggle is fine; dismissing the ruling is not. Communities do the opposite, tolerating disobedience as long as no one complains.

outline.heading: Al-Ghazali: finding prayer hard is a sign of faith
outline.gist: Struggling shows you are striving; ease comes later with closeness to Allah.

outline.heading: No endless explanations before obeying
outline.gist: Islam never commands the irrational, but demanding a full rationale for every ruling gets you nowhere.

outline.heading: Why the punchline sits in the middle
outline.gist: Long surahs divided into chapters place their key verse in the middle after enough build-up.

outline.heading: Clear misguidance: taking what you like
outline.gist: Disobeying is choosing a misguided path; examine where you have mixed convenient culture into the religion.

outline.heading: Parents who demand birr but do not practise it
outline.gist: Show your children how to honour parents by honouring your own.

outline.heading: Zayd's abduction as a child
outline.gist: Zayd, of an Arab lineage, was seized in a raid at six or seven and sold.

outline.heading: From Hakim to Khadijah to the Prophet
outline.gist: Hakim ibn Hizam gave him to Khadijah, who gave him to the Prophet when Zayd was eight.

outline.heading: The worst day that became the best
outline.gist: His abduction led him to the Prophet, the best thing in his life.

outline.heading: Patience can turn the worst experience into a blessing
outline.gist: Years later his family found him and came to Makkah to buy his freedom.

outline.heading: Zayd chooses the Prophet over his father
outline.gist: Offered his freedom at no cost, the teenage Zayd refused to leave, saying he had seen goodness from no one else.

outline.heading: Adopted at the Ka'bah, then married to Zaynab
outline.gist: The Prophet declared him Zayd ibn Muhammad and later married him to his cousin Zaynab bint Jahsh.

outline.heading: Strains in the marriage: the name change
outline.gist: When adoption was abolished he became Zayd ibn Harithah again, which mattered greatly to Zaynab's sense of lineage.

outline.heading: Wealth, children and quarrels
outline.gist: He was poor, she came from a rich family, they had no children, and arguments grew; learning from companions' mistakes does not lower their status.

18:17.ar: ۞وَتَرَى ٱلشَّمۡسَ إِذَا طَلَعَت تَّزَٰوَرُ عَن كَهۡفِهِمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلۡيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَت تَّقۡرِضُهُمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ وَهُمۡ فِي فَجۡوَةࣲ مِّنۡهُۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۗ مَن يَهۡدِ ٱللَّهُ فَهُوَ ٱلۡمُهۡتَدِۖ وَمَن يُضۡلِلۡ فَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُۥ وَلِيࣰّ ا مُّرۡشِدࣰ ا
18:17.en: And thou mightest have seen the sun when it rose move away from their cave to the right, and when it set go past them on the left, and they were in the cleft thereof. That was (one) of the portents of Allah. He whom Allah guideth, he indeed is led aright, and he whom He sendeth astray, for him thou wilt not find a guiding friend

18:18.ar: وَتَحۡسَبُهُمۡ أَيۡقَاظࣰ ا وَهُمۡ رُقُودࣱۚ وَنُقَلِّبُهُمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلۡيَمِينِ وَذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِۖ وَكَلۡبُهُم بَٰسِطࣱ ذِرَاعَيۡهِ بِٱلۡوَصِيدِۚ لَوِ ٱطَّلَعۡتَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ لَوَلَّيۡتَ مِنۡهُمۡ فِرَارࣰ ا وَلَمُلِئۡتَ مِنۡهُمۡ رُعۡبࣰ ا
18:18.en: And thou wouldst have deemed them waking though they were asleep, and We caused them to turn over to the right and the left, and their dog stretching out his paws on the threshold. If thou hadst observed them closely thou hadst assuredly turned away from them in flight, and hadst been filled with awe of them

18:19.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ بَعَثۡنَٰهُمۡ لِيَتَسَآءَلُواْ بَيۡنَهُمۡۚ قَالَ قَآئِلࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ كَمۡ لَبِثۡتُمۡۖ قَالُواْ لَبِثۡنَا يَوۡمًا أَوۡ بَعۡضَ يَوۡمࣲۚ قَالُواْ رَبُّكُمۡ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثۡتُمۡ فَٱبۡعَثُوٓاْ أَحَدَكُم بِوَرِقِكُمۡ هَٰذِهِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ فَلۡيَنظُرۡ أَيُّهَآ أَزۡكَىٰ طَعَامࣰ ا فَلۡيَأۡتِكُم بِرِزۡقࣲ مِّنۡهُ وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ وَلَا يُشۡعِرَنَّ بِكُمۡ أَحَدًا
18:19.en: And in like manner We awakened them that they might question one another. A speaker from among them said: How long have ye tarried? They said: We have tarried a day or some part of a day, (Others) said: Your Lord best knoweth what ye have tarried. Now send one of you with this your silver coin unto the city, and let him see what food is purest there and bring you a supply thereof. Let him be courteous and let no man know of you

18:20.ar: إِنَّهُمۡ إِن يَظۡهَرُواْ عَلَيۡكُمۡ يَرۡجُمُوكُمۡ أَوۡ يُعِيدُوكُمۡ فِي مِلَّتِهِمۡ وَلَن تُفۡلِحُوٓاْ إِذًا أَبَدࣰ ا
18:20.en: For they, if they should come to know of you, will stone you or turn you back to their religion; then ye will never prosper

18:21.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ أَعۡثَرۡنَا عَلَيۡهِمۡ لِيَعۡلَمُوٓاْ أَنَّ وَعۡدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقࣱّ وَأَنَّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ لَا رَيۡبَ فِيهَآ إِذۡ يَتَنَٰزَعُونَ بَيۡنَهُمۡ أَمۡرَهُمۡۖ فَقَالُواْ ٱبۡنُواْ عَلَيۡهِم بُنۡيَٰنࣰ اۖ رَّبُّهُمۡ أَعۡلَمُ بِهِمۡۚ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ غَلَبُواْ عَلَىٰٓ أَمۡرِهِمۡ لَنَتَّخِذَنَّ عَلَيۡهِم مَّسۡجِدࣰ ا
18:21.en: And in like manner We disclosed them (to the people of the city) that they might know that the promise of Allah is true, and that, as for the Hour, there is no doubt concerning it. When (the people of the city) disputed of their case among themselves, they said: Build over them a building; their Lord knoweth best concerning them. Those who won their point said: We verily shall build a place of worship over them

18:9.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتَ أَنَّ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡكَهۡفِ وَٱلرَّقِيمِ كَانُواْ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِنَا عَجَبًا
18:9.en: Or deemest thou that the People of the Cave and the Inscription are a wonder among Our portents

18:14.ar: وَرَبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ إِذۡ قَامُواْ فَقَالُواْ رَبُّنَا رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ لَن نَّدۡعُوَاْ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَٰهࣰ اۖ لَّقَدۡ قُلۡنَآ إِذࣰ ا شَطَطًا
18:14.en: And We made firm their hearts when they stood forth and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We cry unto no Allah beside Him, for then should we utter an enormity
